title: The Aseity of God
speaker: Elder Nick Anderson
series: Anxiety and the Character of God

outline.title: The Biblical Framework for Anxiety
subpoints: Contrast between secular medical views and biblical heart issues
Anxiety as a sin of self-reliance rather than a victimhood
The necessity of repentance and faith over mere coping mechanisms

outline.title: Practical Steps for Peace
subpoints: Finding comfort in God rather than self
Casting burdens on the Lord through prayer
Focusing the mind on Christ to guard the heart

outline.title: Defining Aseity
subpoints: God as a necessary being who cannot not be
Distinction between contingent creatures and the self-existent God

outline.title: The Comfort of God's Self-Sufficiency
subpoints: God’s absolute sufficiency in every aspect of His being
The assurance that God does not need creation to exist
Understanding God's ability to care for believers based on His nature

summary:
This lesson continues the Sunday school series on anxiety by contrasting secular and biblical frameworks for understanding worry. While secular views often treat anxiety as a medical condition requiring medication, the biblical perspective identifies it as a heart issue rooted in self-reliance and a lack of trust in God. The sermon emphasizes that anxiety is a sin of unbelief, requiring repentance and a deliberate shift in focus from self to Christ. Practical steps for overcoming anxiety include finding comfort in God, casting burdens through prayer, and maintaining a mind stayed upon Him, as promised in Scripture.

The primary theological focus is the attribute of aseity, defined as God’s self-existence. Drawing on Thomas Aquinas and R.C. Sproul, the teaching explains that God is a necessary being who exists independently of any external cause. Unlike contingent beings who depend on other factors for their existence, God is absolutely sufficient in Himself. This truth is revealed in Exodus 3:14, where God identifies Himself as "I AM." Understanding God’s aseity provides profound comfort, assuring believers that God’s care and ability to sustain them are grounded in His eternal, self-existent nature rather than any external circumstance.
